chapter.name: The Rise of the Marathas
chapter.blurb: Under Theme B, Tapestry of the Past. The Marathas of the Deccan plateau, identified by the Marathi language, are given a cultural foundation by the bhakti saints before Chhatrapati Shivaji (born 1630) unites them. From his father's jagir at Pune he takes neglected forts, builds the first real Indian navy of the age, and uses guerrilla warfare against Afzal Khan of Bijapur, Shaista Khan and the Mughals, sacking Surat, conceding Purandar, escaping from Agra in a basket, and being crowned at Raigad in 1674 with the ideal of Swarajya. After his death Sambhaji is executed, Rajaram moves the fight to Gingee and Tarabai turns the Marathas onto the offensive; the state decentralises, the Peshwas lead a pan-Indian expansion to Delhi and Peshawar, survive Panipat in 1761, and are finally ended by the British in the three Anglo-Maratha wars of 1775-1818. The chapter then sets out Maratha administration (salaried and transferred officials, the council of eight ministers, chauth and sardeshmukhi, bargirs and shiledars, forts, Kanhoji Angre's navy, panchayat justice, roads and sea trade) and the cultural revival -- Chhatrapati Shivaji's Sanskrit seal, the Rajya-Vyavahara-Kosha, the Modi script, Tarabai and Ahilyabai Holkar, and Thanjavur under Ekoji and Serfoji II -- closing with the Maratha legacy as an early seed of India's freedom movement.

scope_in.item: Identify who the Marathas are: a people of the Deccan plateau and present-day Maharashtra, named for the Marathi language and its literary history since the 12th century
State that 13th-century Maharashtra was ruled by the Yadava dynasty from Devagiri, present-day Daulatabad, and that the Khilji Sultanate from Delhi overcame it in the early 14th century

Explain how the bhakti tradition, its saints from diverse sections of society, and translations of the Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita into Marathi gave society a cultural foundation that later helped the Marathas organise politically
Describe Chhatrapati Shivaji's birth in 1630 in the Bhonsle clan to Shahji and Jijabai, his upbringing in the jagir at Pune, his first campaigns at sixteen, and the growing idea of Swarajya
Explain why the Maratha navy was a revolutionary step, and define guerrilla warfare and apply it to the killing of Afzal Khan at Pratapgad and the wagh nakh
Recount the night raid on Shaista Khan's camp as a surgical strike, the sacking of Surat, the treaty at Purandar with Jai Singh, and the escape from house arrest at Agra in baskets
Describe the 1674 coronation at Raigad with full Vedic rites, the title Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati and the Rajyabhisheka shaka era, and the dakshina-digvijaya that gave the Marathas strategic depth
State Chhatrapati Shivaji's stand against the Dutch slave trade, his death at fifty, and his influence on Chhatrasal of Bundelkhand and the poet Bhushan
Trace the Marathas after Chhatrapati Shivaji: Sambhaji's execution and the fall of Raigad, Rajaram at Gingee, Aurangzeb's failure in the Deccan, and Tarabai's inroads into Mughal territory
Explain the shift from a centralised state to a decentralised one and the rise of the Peshwa, with Bajirao I and Nanasaheb Peshwa leading the pan-Indian expansion

Recount the northward expansion to Lahore, Attock and Peshawar, the defeat at Panipat in 1761, the recovery under Madhavrao I, Mahadji Shinde's recapture of Delhi in 1771, and the three Anglo-Maratha wars of 1775-1818 with the reasons for the British success
State that Nana Phadnavis organised the first pan-Indian anti-British alliance with Hyder Ali of Mysore and the Nizam of Hyderabad

Describe Maratha civilian administration: abolition of hereditary posts and land assignments, salaries from the state treasury, periodic transfers, pensions to soldiers' widows, coins in his own name in Devanagari, and the ashta pradhana mandala of eight ministers
Explain chauth at 25 per cent and sardeshmukhi at a further 10 per cent, what the Marathas gave in return, and how some such provinces joined the empire

Describe military administration: infantry, cavalry and navy; bargirs and shiledars; European-style troops and artillery in the 18th century; swords, lances, guns and rockets; and forts as the core of the state in Ramachandrapant Amatya's Adnyapatra
Explain Maratha maritime supremacy under Kanhoji Angre, the European cartaz trade passes, the Marathas demanding passes in turn, and the 1665 episode at Muscat

Describe the judicial system -- moderation in capital punishment, the panchayat as the main body of justice, appeal to a chief, and the kotwal in towns -- and the trade networks of ships, roads, ferries and bridges

Explain the cultural revival: the Sanskrit seal instead of a Persian one, the Rajya-Vyavahara-Kosha reducing foreign loanwords, the saffron flag, rebuilt temples, and the Modi script for correspondence

Describe Tarabai as the architect of the northward expansion and Ahilyabai Holkar's thirty years of rule, her temples, ghats, wells and roads from Kedarnath to Rameswaram, and the Maheshwar weaving industry

Describe Thanjavur under Ekoji and Serfoji II: the syncretic multilingual culture, Devendra Kuravanji, Carnatic music and early Bharatanatyam, the Dhanwantari Mahal, the printing press, and the Brihadishwara temple inscription

State the Maratha legacy: the largest Indian empire before the British, efficient administration, revival of local traditions without religious discrimination, and Swarajya as an early seed of the freedom movement

scope_out.item: Detailed campaign-by-campaign history of the Maratha expansion across India
scope_out.reason: The chapter itself defers this on page 70: 'You may study about Marathas campaign in detail in the higher classes'

scope_out.item: British colonial rule in India and the Indian freedom movement

scope_out.reason: Named on pages 63-64 only as background; the book sets this as a Let's Explore activity, not as taught content

scope_out.reason: Mentioned on page 79 only as taking shape under Serfoji II's patronage

scope_out.item: Hyder Ali of Mysore and the Nizam of Hyderabad as rulers of their own states
scope_out.reason: Named on page 71 only as Nana Phadnavis's allies in the anti-British alliance

concepts.name: Who the Marathas were and the bhakti foundation
concepts.description: The Marathas of the Deccan and Maharashtra, the Marathi language, Yadava and Khilji rule, and how the bhakti saints gave society the cultural foundation on which Maratha political power was later built.
concepts.idea: Long before the Marathas became a political power, they already shared a land, a language and a devotional culture.
concepts.rule: The Marathas are native to the Deccan plateau, more specifically present-day Maharashtra, and are identified with Marathi, which has had a continuous literary history since the 12th century. In the 13th century most of Maharashtra was ruled by the Yadava dynasty from Devagiri, present-day Daulatabad, until the Khilji Sultanate from Delhi overcame it in the early 14th century. Amid these changes the bhakti tradition continued: between the 7th and 17th centuries saints from diverse sections of society preferred devotion to merely external ritualism and composed songs and poetry in the languages of the masses, so their message travelled far and wide.
concepts.example: Saints such as Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Tukaram and Ramdas translated texts like the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita into Marathi, and some worked on social organisation and political awareness, similar to the Sikh gurus.

questions.a: The Deccan plateau

questions.a: So that their message could travel far and wide among ordinary people

o: Merely external ritualism

questions.q: What does the chapter mean by 'literary history', and which language does it use as its example?
questions.a: Literary history is the historical development of writings in prose or poetry in a particular language. The chapter's example is Marathi, which has had a rich and continuous literary history since the 12th century.
s: Defines literary history as the development of writings in prose or poetry in a language
Names Marathi and its continuous history since the 12th century

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) The bhakti saints of Maharashtra helped translate texts such as the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita into Marathi. (II) The bhakti saints of this period all came from the same section of society. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I
o: Only I
Only II
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

questions.q: How did the bhakti movement in Maharashtra prepare the ground for the later rise of Maratha political power?
questions.a: The saints spread devotional ideas in Marathi and made important texts accessible, and some of them also worked on social organisation and political awareness. Society therefore acquired a solid cultural foundation, which later helped the Marathas organise themselves into a political power.
s: Saints built a shared cultural foundation through Marathi devotional writing
Links that foundation to the Marathas later organising as a political power

questions.q: The chapter says some Maharashtrian saints resembled the Sikh gurus. In which respect?
questions.a: Some of them also worked on social organisation and political awareness
o: Some of them also worked on social organisation and political awareness
They both wrote mainly in Persian
They both led armies against the Mughals
They both founded sultanates in the Deccan

questions.q: A student writes that the Marathas first became a political power in the 13th century. Correct this using the chapter.
questions.a: In the 13th century Maharashtra was ruled by the Yadava dynasty, not by the Marathas as a political power. Maratha chiefs made early attempts at sovereignty only in the 17th century, and those failed until Chhatrapati Shivaji rose and brought the Marathas together.
s: Identifies the 13th century as the period of Yadava rule
Names Chhatrapati Shivaji and the 17th century as when Maratha power actually began

questions.q: Which of these developments came last in time?
questions.a: Chhatrapati Shivaji bringing the Marathas together
o: Chhatrapati Shivaji bringing the Marathas together
The beginning of Marathi's literary history
Yadava rule over Maharashtra from Devagiri
The Khilji Sultanate overcoming the Yadava dynasty

questions.q: The chapter says the bhakti saints came 'from diverse sections of society'. Explain why that mattered for how far their message spread.
questions.a: Because the saints came from many different sections of society and composed in the language ordinary people spoke rather than in a scholarly language only, people of every background could hear and understand them, so the message travelled far and wide.
s: Notes their diverse origins and their use of the language of the masses
States the effect: the message reached ordinary people across society

questions.q: Using only this chapter, set out the political changes Maharashtra passed through between the 13th and the 17th centuries.
questions.a: In the 13th century most of Maharashtra was under the Yadava dynasty with its capital at Devagiri. In the early 14th century the Yadavas were overcome by the Khilji Sultanate from Delhi. By the 17th century some Maratha chiefs were making early attempts at sovereignty, but these failed until Chhatrapati Shivaji united the Marathas.
s: Yadava rule from Devagiri in the 13th century
The Khilji Sultanate from Delhi overcomes the Yadavas in the early 14th century
Unsuccessful 17th-century Maratha attempts, then Chhatrapati Shivaji

questions.q: Bhakti spread across many parts of India between the 7th and 17th centuries, yet this chapter connects it to Maratha political power in particular. Apply the chapter's reasoning to explain that connection.
questions.a: Sample: In Maharashtra the saints wrote in Marathi, the language of the whole region, so a single shared culture formed across the Deccan countryside. Some of these saints went further than devotion and worked on social organisation and political awareness. The result was a society already bound together and already used to thinking about its own organisation, so when Chhatrapati Shivaji called for Swarajya there was a people ready to be united, not just an army to be raised.
s: Notes that the Maharashtrian saints wrote in Marathi, creating a shared regional culture
Notes that some saints worked on social organisation and political awareness
Connects this foundation to the Marathas' later ability to organise politically

questions.q: Assertion (A): The chapter treats the bhakti tradition of Maharashtra as part of the background to Maratha political power. Reason (R): The saints gave society a solid cultural foundation, and some of them also worked on social organisation and political awareness. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The chapter says that 'amidst such political changes, the cultural traditions continued'. Analyse what this tells us about the relationship between rulers and culture in this period.
questions.a: Sample: Rulers changed twice in this account -- the Yadavas fell to the Khilji Sultanate -- yet bhakti went on without a break. Culture in this period therefore did not depend on who held the throne; it lived in the saints, the songs and the language of ordinary people. That is why it could outlast a conquest and still be there, centuries later, for the Marathas to build on.
s: Names the changes of ruler, from Yadava to Khilji Sultanate
Argues that the bhakti tradition continued independently of who ruled
Draws the conclusion that culture outlasted rulers and was available to the Marathas later

questions.q: The chapter identifies the Marathas by their language rather than only by the territory they held. Analyse why a shared language can hold a people together more firmly than a shared ruler.
questions.a: Sample: A ruler can be defeated, as the Yadavas were, and then the people under him have nothing left in common; but Marathi was spoken by everybody in the region and had a written literature going back to the 12th century, so it survived every change of throne. The bhakti saints then used that same language to carry ideas to every section of society. A language is therefore held by the people themselves rather than by a court, which is why the chapter uses it, and not a kingdom, to say who the Marathas were.
s: Notes that rulers can be overthrown while the language remains
Uses the chapter's evidence: Marathi's long literary history and the saints' use of it
Concludes that a language belongs to the people rather than to a court

questions.q: 'Without the bhakti saints there would have been no Maratha empire.' Judge how far this chapter supports that claim.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter does support part of it: it says the society acquired a solid cultural foundation from the saints, which later helped the Marathas organise themselves into a political power. But it does not say the saints were enough on their own -- it also records that Maratha chiefs tried and failed to establish sovereignty in the 17th century, and that success came only when Chhatrapati Shivaji brought them together. So the saints are best read as a necessary background rather than the whole cause.
s: Gives the evidence in favour: the cultural foundation that helped them organise
Gives the evidence against: earlier Maratha attempts failed until Chhatrapati Shivaji
Reaches a judgement that weighs both sides

questions.q: Design a two-panel museum display called 'Before Chhatrapati Shivaji' covering pages 62 to 64. Say what each panel shows and write a one-line caption for each.
questions.a: Sample: Panel 1, 'A land and its rulers': a map of the Deccan with Devagiri marked, and the Yadava dynasty giving way to the Khilji Sultanate. Caption -- 'Thrones changed hands at Devagiri, but the people and their language stayed.' Panel 2, 'Songs in Marathi': images of Sant Tukaram and Sant Ramdas with a page of Marathi verse. Caption -- 'Saints put the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita into the language of the masses, and the message travelled far.'
s: Panel 1 is described with content drawn from the chapter
Panel 2 is described with content drawn from the chapter
Both captions are single lines that fit their panel and the chapter

concepts.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji's rise, Swarajya, the navy and guerrilla warfare
concepts.description: Chhatrapati Shivaji's birth and upbringing at Pune, his first campaigns and forts, the vision of Swarajya, the founding of the Maratha navy and the use of guerrilla warfare against Afzal Khan at Pratapgad.
concepts.idea: A boy with a small jagir built a sovereign kingdom by taking forts, using the land itself as a weapon, and putting ships on a coast nobody else was guarding.
concepts.rule: Chhatrapati Shivaji was born in 1630 in the Bhonsle clan to Shahji and Jijabai and grew up in the jagir at Pune under Jijabai and trusted officials. At sixteen he began capturing neglected and unoccupied forts, and his vision of a sovereign kingdom, or Swarajya, grew to cover political, economic and cultural life. When his kingdom reached the west coast he built a navy to secure the resources of the coastal regions -- a revolutionary step, since the Bijapur Sultanate kept only merchant ships and even the Mughals used a navy very little. Against larger armies he used guerrilla warfare, which uses small groups with speed, surprise and knowledge of the terrain.
concepts.example: Bijapur sent the veteran general Afzal Khan; Chhatrapati Shivaji met him at the foot of Pratapgad fort amid thick forests, killed him with the wagh nakh, and the Marathas hidden in the mountains routed the Khan's army.

questions.q: Chhatrapati Shivaji was born in 1630 into which clan?
questions.a: The Bhonsle clan
o: The Bhonsle clan
The Holkar dynasty
The Adil Shahi dynasty
The Yadava dynasty

questions.a: His mother Jijabai, with some trusted officials
o: His mother Jijabai, with some trusted officials

questions.a: wagh nakh

questions.a: Sixteen
o: Sixteen

questions.q: What did 'Swarajya' mean as Chhatrapati Shivaji used it?
questions.a: A sovereign kingdom of his own, extending to political, economic and cultural life
o: A sovereign kingdom of his own, extending to political, economic and cultural life
A tax of one quarter of the revenue of a province
A council of eight ministers who advised the king
A pass that a ship had to buy before trading

questions.q: Guerrilla warfare, as this chapter defines it, uses
questions.a: Small groups with speed, surprise and knowledge of the terrain to defeat bigger armies
o: Small groups with speed, surprise and knowledge of the terrain to defeat bigger armies
Large disciplined infantry formations trained in the European style
Long sieges that starve a fort into surrender
Heavy artillery bombardment from a safe distance

questions.q: What was a jagir, and what was its holder allowed to do with it?
questions.a: A jagir was a piece of land given by a king or ruler to someone, usually a noble or a soldier, as a reward for service. The person who received it could collect taxes from that land and use the money for his own needs or to help the king when needed.
s: Land granted by a ruler as a reward for service
The holder could collect taxes from that land and use the money

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) The Bijapur Sultanate kept merchant ships but had no full-time naval force to protect its coast. (II) The Mughal Empire maintained a large standing navy at this time. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I
o: Only I
Only II
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

questions.q: Why does the chapter call the building of a Maratha navy 'a truly revolutionary step at the time'?
questions.a: Because no power around him kept a proper navy: the Bijapur Sultanate maintained merchant ships but no full-time naval force to protect the coast, and even the Mughal Empire's use of a navy was very limited. Chhatrapati Shivaji built one so that he could secure access to the resources of the coastal regions his kingdom had reached.
s: No comparable Indian naval force existed, in Bijapur or under the Mughals
His purpose was to secure the west coast and its resources

questions.q: Chhatrapati Shivaji began by capturing forts that were neglected and unoccupied. Which result does the chapter connect to this choice?
questions.a: He consolidated his hold over the Pune region and strengthened those forts' defences
o: He consolidated his hold over the Pune region and strengthened those forts' defences
He gained control of all the west-coast ports at once
He forced Aurangzeb to leave the Deccan
He ended the infighting between the Deccan sultans

questions.q: The meeting with Afzal Khan was arranged at the foot of Pratapgad fort amid thick forests. Explain why that setting suited the Marathas.
questions.a: Hilly, forested country was exactly the terrain the Maratha style of fighting depended on, since guerrilla warfare uses knowledge of the ground, speed and surprise. It also let the Maratha soldiers stay hidden in the mountains, so that once Afzal Khan was killed they could fall on his army and rout it.
s: Forest and hills suited guerrilla tactics, which rely on knowledge of the terrain
Marathas hidden in the mountains could rout the Khan's army

questions.q: Why did the Bijapur Sultanate send the veteran general Afzal Khan against Chhatrapati Shivaji?
questions.a: His successes had invited the wrath of the sultanate
o: His successes had invited the wrath of the sultanate
He had sacked the port city of Surat
He had begun demanding naval trade passes from the Europeans
He had crowned himself at Raigad

questions.q: Apply the chapter's definition of guerrilla warfare to the defeat of Afzal Khan's army.
questions.a: The Marathas used a small force rather than a large one, kept it hidden in the mountains around Pratapgad, and struck by surprise immediately after Afzal Khan was killed. Speed, surprise and knowledge of the forested, hilly terrain let them rout an army much bigger than their own, which is exactly what the chapter says guerrilla warfare does.
s: Identifies small groups, surprise and use of hilly forested terrain
States the outcome: a much larger army was routed

questions.q: A small kingdom finds itself beside a far larger and richer neighbour. Using three things Chhatrapati Shivaji actually did in these pages, suggest how it might survive.
questions.a: First, take and strengthen forts, as he did with the neglected forts around Pune, because forts let a small force hold ground. Second, avoid open battle and fight in the guerrilla style, using small groups, speed, surprise and knowledge of the terrain. Third, secure the coast with ships of its own, as he did when his kingdom reached the west coast, so that resources and trade are not left to the enemy.
s: Capture and strengthen forts
Use guerrilla tactics rather than open battle
Build a navy to secure the coast and its resources

questions.q: The chapter says the constant infighting of the Deccan sultans caused much hardship for the common people of the Pune region. Apply the idea of Swarajya to explain what Chhatrapati Shivaji offered such people that the sultans did not.
questions.a: Sample: The sultans fought each other and the people of Pune paid the price, because no one power was answerable for the region. Swarajya meant a kingdom of their own, governed from within rather than fought over from outside, and it covered economic and cultural life as well as politics. So what he offered was not merely a change of master but an end to being the ground on which other people's quarrels were settled.
s: States the hardship caused by the sultans' infighting
Explains Swarajya as self-rule covering political, economic and cultural life
Draws the contrast: rule from within instead of being a battleground

questions.q: Assertion (A): Chhatrapati Shivaji felt the need to establish a navy once his kingdom expanded to India's west coast. Reason (R): He wanted to secure access to the resources of the coastal regions. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Analyse why taking forts, rather than seeking open battles, was the sensible first move for a sixteen-year-old with a small following.
questions.a: Sample: At sixteen he had no army large enough to meet a sultanate in the field, so an open battle would have decided everything at once and against him. The forts he chose were neglected and unoccupied, which meant they could be taken cheaply and then strengthened. Each fort held a piece of country and a route, so his power grew step by step, and the hilly ground around them was the same terrain his guerrilla tactics depended on.
s: Notes that his force was too small for open battle
Notes that neglected and unoccupied forts could be taken cheaply and strengthened
Links fort-holding to controlling territory and to guerrilla tactics

questions.q: Compare the Maratha navy with the merchant ships of the Bijapur Sultanate, and analyse what the difference shows about how each power saw the sea.
questions.a: Sample: Bijapur kept merchant ships, so for it the sea was a road for goods and nothing more; it had no full-time force to protect that coast. Chhatrapati Shivaji built a fighting navy and naval fortifications such as Sindhudurg, so for him the sea was a frontier of the kingdom that had to be held. The difference is that one power treated the coast as a place to trade from and the other treated it as territory, which is why the chapter calls his step revolutionary.
s: States what Bijapur had: merchant ships and no full-time naval force
States what the Marathas built: a fighting navy and coastal fortifications
Draws the conclusion about the sea as trade route versus defended frontier

questions.q: Was the killing of Afzal Khan a genuine military success or merely a trick? Judge this using evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: It can be called a trick, since the one-on-one meeting was arranged by Chhatrapati Shivaji and his advisers and he came armed with the wagh nakh. But the chapter shows it was more than that: Bijapur had sent a veteran general against him with a large army, and the killing was only the opening of a planned action in which Maratha troops hidden in the mountains routed that army with guerrilla attacks. Judged as a whole it was a military operation that used surprise, which is what guerrilla warfare is, rather than a trick standing on its own.
s: States the case for calling it a trick, using the arranged meeting and the wagh nakh
States the case against, using the planned rout of the Khan's army
Reaches a judgement grounded in the chapter's definition of guerrilla warfare

questions.q: Write the four-line entry a Maratha soldier might have made in a fort logbook on the day after the fight at Pratapgad, using only details from these pages.
questions.a: Sample: 'We waited in the mountains above Pratapgad since dawn, as ordered. The Bijapur general Afzal Khan came down to the meeting place below the fort, in the thick forest. Our master killed him there with the tiger's claw. We came down on the Khan's army from the slopes and scattered it before evening.'
s: Written as a soldier's short first-person entry
Uses correct details: Pratapgad, the forest meeting, Afzal Khan, the wagh nakh
Includes the guerrilla attack from the mountains and its result

concepts.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji against the Mughals, the coronation and the southern conquest
concepts.description: The night raid on Shaista Khan, the sacking of Surat, the treaty at Purandar, the escape from Agra, the coronation of 1674 at Raigad, the dakshina-digvijaya, and Chhatrapati Shivaji's death and influence.
concepts.idea: Chhatrapati Shivaji turned every Mughal blow into an opportunity, and then made his kingdom formally sovereign by crowning himself.
concepts.rule: After Shaista Khan invaded his territories for three years, Chhatrapati Shivaji raided the Khan's camp at night with only a few soldiers -- a raid the chapter compares to a modern surgical strike. He then sacked the wealthy Mughal port of Surat, taking treasure worth almost one crore rupees while sparing religious places. Aurangzeb sent Jai Singh, who forced the treaty of Purandar; persuaded to visit Agra, Chhatrapati Shivaji was insulted and placed under house arrest, and escaped hidden in gift baskets. In 1674 he was crowned with full Vedic rites at Raigad as Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati and began his own era, the Rajyabhisheka shaka.
concepts.example: The dakshina-digvijaya, the conquest of the South, took in the then ill-defended region of present-day northern Tamil Nadu and parts of Karnataka, which later gave the Marathas great strategic depth against the Mughal invasion.

questions.q: Apply the chapter's definition of a surgical strike to the night raid on Shaista Khan's camp, pointing to the features that match.
questions.a: A surgical strike is an attack meant to damage only a specific target with no or minimal damage to other people or property. The raid matches this: Chhatrapati Shivaji went in with only a few soldiers, struck the Khan's camp at night rather than fighting his whole army, and the result was that the Khan himself barely escaped, losing a few fingers, and left Maharashtra.

questions.q: The chapter says Chhatrapati Shivaji's stand against the Dutch slave trade showed deep concern for his subjects. Set out the situation he stepped into and why the chapter treats his action as remarkable.
questions.a: While he was in the South, most Europeans were capturing Indians and selling them as slaves. They met no opposition at all from any Indian power, so the trade went on unchecked. Chhatrapati Shivaji forbade the Dutch from trading slaves, and the chapter treats this as remarkable because he was the first Indian ruler to intervene, which showed he counted ordinary people as his responsibility.

questions.a: Sample: Europeans in India watched him beat two great powers in turn -- Bijapur at Pratapgad and the Mughals at Surat and Agra -- while holding far smaller resources than either. questions.a: Sample: A battle wins land, but it leaves a ruler looking like a successful commander who might be beaten next season. The coronation at Raigad made him Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati by formal rite, so his authority rested on law and religion rather than only on the last victory. Starting the Rajyabhisheka shaka went further still: dating time itself from his reign announced that a new sovereign power had begun, which is a claim no single battle can make.
s: Contrasts what a battle wins with what a formal ceremony confers

The escape from Agra is given no such foreign notice, but the chapter does say Aurangzeb could never capture him again, and it was his struggle against the Mughals that inspired Chhatrasal in Bundelkhand and drew the poet Bhushan to Maharashtra. On the chapter's own evidence Surat travelled further abroad, while Agra counted for more within India.

concepts.name: The Marathas after Chhatrapati Shivaji: Peshwas, expansion and the Anglo-Maratha wars
concepts.description: Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai against Aurangzeb, the shift to a decentralised state under the Peshwas, the pan-Indian expansion to Delhi and Peshawar, Panipat 1761, and the three Anglo-Maratha wars that ended Maratha power.
concepts.idea: After Chhatrapati Shivaji the Marathas survived their worst crisis, then spread across India under the Peshwas, and finally lost not to the Mughals but to the British.
concepts.rule: Sambhaji became Chhatrapati and was captured and executed by Aurangzeb, who also took Raigad; Rajaram then moved the fight to Gingee, and Aurangzeb died in the Deccan without subduing the Marathas. Under Tarabai the Marathas went onto the offensive. The centralised state gave way to a decentralised one, still nominally under the Chhatrapati but with the chiefs and above all the Peshwa, a Persian term for prime minister, holding real power. Bajirao I and Nanasaheb Peshwa led the pan-Indian expansion; after the defeat at Panipat in 1761 the Marathas recovered under Madhavrao I and Mahadji Shinde retook Delhi in 1771. Three Anglo-Maratha wars between 1775 and 1818 ended Maratha power.
concepts.example: The chapter concludes that, in effect, the British took India from the Marathas more than from the Mughals or any other power.

questions.a: Realising that with Aurangzeb and the Mughal army tied down in the Deccan the north was unprotected, she organised large Maratha armies and sent them into Mughal territories. Under Rajaram they survived by moving south to Gingee, defending their forts staunchly and often holding the upper hand in skirmishes, so that Aurangzeb died without subduing them. Under Tarabai they went onto the attack, sending large armies into unprotected Mughal territory in the north and eventually conquering large parts of India.

questions.q: Analyse both the advantages and the dangers of the decentralised Maratha structure of the 18th century.
questions.a: Sample: The advantage was reach. Chiefs with power of their own could campaign far from Maharashtra without waiting on orders, which is how the Marathas came to hold Delhi and press as far as Peshawar, and how they brought large parts of India under control and generally ruled them well. The danger was that the same autonomy left the centre unable to correct a chief who misused it, so there was occasional indiscipline and abuse, in stark contrast with Chhatrapati Shivaji's values, and the chiefs could pull in different directions.

questions.a: Sample: Decentralisation worked while the chiefs pointed the same way: each could raise and lead forces in his own region, and that is how the Marathas spread from Maharashtra to Delhi and beyond. But power that does not depend on the centre also does not answer to it. The chapter names increased internal disunity as one of the two causes of the British victory, the other being British organisational and technological superiority. The British could face the chiefs in turn rather than a single Maratha state, so the very structure that carried the Marathas across India left them without one voice when it mattered.
s: Explains how autonomous chiefs made the wide expansion possible

The Marathas defended their fortresses, often had the upper hand in battles and skirmishes, and kept Aurangzeb in the Deccan until he died there without subduing them. They then emerged as a strong contender to the Mughals and, under Tarabai, invaded Mughal territory themselves. The campaign wounded them badly and left them stronger in standing.
s: Gives the evidence for the claim: Sambhaji's execution and the fall of Raigad

concepts.name: Maratha administration: civilian, military, maritime, judicial and trade
concepts.description: Salaried and transferred officials, the council of eight ministers, chauth and sardeshmukhi, the three arms of the forces, bargirs and shiledars, forts, Kanhoji Angre's navy and the trade passes, panchayat justice, and the roads, ferries and sea trade.
concepts.idea: The Marathas held their empire together with paid officials, taxed protection, forts and ships rather than with hereditary lords.
concepts.rule: Chhatrapati Shivaji abolished hereditary posts and land assignments, paid every official a salary from the state treasury and transferred officials periodically so that none could dictate terms to the king; an ashta pradhana mandala of eight ministers assisted him. From provinces not directly under them the Marathas levied chauth at 25 per cent and sardeshmukhi at a further 10 per cent, giving protection and non-interference in return. The forces had three arms -- infantry, cavalry and navy -- the cavalry made up of bargirs, equipped by the state, and shiledars, who equipped themselves. Forts were the core of the state, justice was delivered by the panchayat with appeal to a chief, and trade moved by ship, road, ferry and bridge.
concepts.example: Ramachandrapant Amatya wrote in the Adnyapatra that the kingdom was created from forts alone, and that it survived Aurangzeb's decades-long onslaught because of them.

questions.a: Sample: A battle is won in one place on one day, and only those present see it. A coin goes everywhere the kingdom trades and stays in circulation for years, so striking one in his own name told every merchant and villager who handled it that there was now a sovereign here. The choice of the Devanagari script carried a second message, since it asserted his cultural identity against the Persian then usual on coins and seals. A coin therefore announces sovereignty and identity continuously, which no single victory can do.
s: Notes that minting in one's own name signified sovereignty
Notes the use of Devanagari as an assertion of cultural identity
Contrasts the lasting, wide reach of a coin with a single battle

questions.q: Analyse how the arrangement of chauth and sardeshmukhi let the Maratha Empire grow without conquering every province it drew revenue from.
questions.a: Sample: A province that was not directly ruled still paid chauth at 25 per cent and sardeshmukhi at a further 10 per cent, and in return the Marathas protected it and left its internal administration alone. That gave the Marathas an income and a military presence across a huge area without the cost of governing or garrisoning it. Because the Mughals approved the arrangement by treaty it also had a legal face, and over time some of these provinces simply became part of the Maratha Empire, so influence turned into territory without a war.

Notes that Mughal treaties legitimised it and some provinces later joined the empire

questions.q: The chapter places trade networks and roads in the same section as armies and forts. Analyse why a state's roads, ferries and bridges belong in an account of its power.
questions.a: Sample: Roads, ferries and bridges are what let anything else move. An army that cannot reach a threatened fort in time cannot defend it, and revenue such as chauth has to be carried from distant provinces to the treasury. The chapter records roads being constructed and maintained, ferries kept for riverine transport in Odisha and bridges built over rivers and streams, all in territories far from Maharashtra. Trade and troops travelled on the same routes, so the same works that made merchants rich also made the empire governable, which is why they sit beside the forts and not apart from them.
s: Explains that roads and river crossings move armies, revenue and goods
Uses the chapter's examples of roads, Odisha's ferries and bridges
Concludes that such infrastructure is part of holding an empire together

questions.q: Chhatrapati Shivaji's letter tells officials to take teak for the navy only with permission, and never to touch mango or jackfruit trees. Judge what this shows about how he wanted officials to treat the subjects.
questions.a: Sample: It shows that he put the people's interests above the convenience of his own officials, even when the navy needed the timber, because permission had to be secured first. His reason is not law but feeling: mango and jackfruit trees take many years to mature and people look after them like their children, so cutting them causes a sorrow that does not end. He then states the principle plainly, that what is accomplished by oppressing others perishes soon along with the oppressor. Taken with his order not to grab even a blade of grass, it shows he judged his officials by how they treated the weakest subject.
s: Notes that even a state need required permission and restraint
Uses his reasoning about the trees and the people who tend them
Draws a judgement about the standard he set for officials

questions.q: Draft a short 'rules for officials' notice as Chhatrapati Shivaji's administration might have issued it, with three rules taken from this chapter.
questions.a: Sample: 'To all officers of this kingdom. One: your post is not hereditary and carries no land. You will draw your salary from the state treasury, and you may be transferred at any time. Two: take nothing from the subjects by force, not even a blade of grass. Timber for the Navy may be cut only with permission, and mango and jackfruit trees are not to be touched. Three: the widow of a soldier who died in battle shall have her pension, and her son may be given a military post.'
s: Written as a short notice addressed to officials
Three rules given, each drawn from the chapter
The rules are accurate to what the chapter actually says

concepts.name: Cultural revival, the Maratha women, Thanjavur and the Maratha legacy
concepts.description: Chhatrapati Shivaji's Sanskrit seal and the Rajya-Vyavahara-Kosha, the Modi script, the revival of local traditions, Tarabai and Ahilyabai Holkar, Thanjavur under Ekoji and Serfoji II, and the legacy the Marathas left to Indian history.
concepts.idea: The Marathas did not only win territory; they gave Indians back a confidence in their own language, faith and arts.
concepts.rule: Chhatrapati Shivaji's seal carried a Sanskrit inscription instead of the usual Persian, and he commissioned the Rajya-Vyavahara-Kosha, which supplied Sanskrit equivalents for Persian diplomatic words so that foreign loanwords in Maratha diplomacy fell considerably. He rebuilt desecrated temples and promoted Sanskrit and Marathi literature while respecting other religions; the Modi script, a cursive Devanagari, was used for correspondence. Maratha women ruled in their own right: Tarabai was the architect of the northward expansion, and Ahilyabai Holkar governed for thirty years and built or restored temples, ghats, wells and roads from Kedarnath to Rameswaram. In the south the Thanjavur Marathas built a syncretic culture.
concepts.example: Serfoji II wrote the Marathi play Devendra Kuravanji, patronised the musicians under whom modern Carnatic music took shape, founded the Dhanwantari Mahal and started the first printing press set up in India by a native ruler.

questions.q: Why does the chapter call Tarabai the architect of the northward Maratha expansion?
questions.a: She realised that with Aurangzeb and the Mughal army held down in the Deccan, north India was left unprotected. Acting on that, she organised large Maratha armies and sent them to invade Mughal territories in the north, which is how the northward expansion began.
s: She saw that north India was unprotected while the Mughals were in the Deccan
She organised and sent large armies north, beginning the expansion

questions.q: Consider these statements about Serfoji II. (I) He established the Dhanwantari Mahal, which offered free treatment using both Indian and Western medicine. (II) He started a printing press, the first such example in India by a native ruler. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Describe the cultural environment of Thanjavur under the Marathas.
questions.a: It was multilingual, with a mix of many influences: the local Tamil culture, the Telugu culture of the former rulers and the Marathi culture of the current rulers all interacted freely. The result was a syncretic culture, rich and full of innovation, with rulers who were themselves poets and dramatists and great patrons of the arts.
s: Names the multilingual mix of Tamil, Telugu and Marathi
Notes the free interaction, the syncretic culture and the patronage of the arts

questions.a: From Kedarnath in the north to Rameswaram in the south
o: From Kedarnath in the north to Rameswaram in the south
From Lahore in the north to Peshawar in the west
From Thanjavur to Gingee in the far south
From Pune to Raigad in the Maratha homeland

questions.q: Give two ways in which the Marathas supported culture outside Maharashtra, using examples from the chapter.
questions.a: The Bhonsles of Nagpur supported local culture and tradition, and the worship of Lord Jagannath at Puri in Odisha, often interrupted during Mughal rule, was revived with Maratha support. In the south, the Thanjavur Marathas patronised the arts, and under Serfoji II modern Carnatic music took shape and Bharatanatyam reached its early stages.

Gives one example from the south, such as the arts at Thanjavur under Serfoji II

questions.a: Chhatrapati Shivaji was a devout Hindu who respected other religions while upholding his own

questions.q: Apply what the chapter says about Serfoji II to explain how one ruler can shape a region's music and dance.
questions.a: Serfoji II patronised many talented musicians, which gave them the support to work and to train others. Because that patronage was sustained, it was during his time that modern Carnatic music took shape and the famous classical dance form of Bharatanatyam passed through its early stages, so a ruler's choice of what to fund decided which art forms grew.
s: Notes that he patronised many talented musicians
Links that patronage to Carnatic music taking shape and early Bharatanatyam

questions.q: Using the chapter, describe three ways in which Ahilyabai Holkar served the people of her kingdom and beyond.
questions.a: She governed the Holkar state for thirty years after losing her husband and her son, administering it wisely while caring for the common people. She built and restored hundreds of temples, ghats, wells and roads throughout India, from Kedarnath in the north to Rameswaram in the south, including the Kashi Vishwanath temple at Varanasi and the Somnath temple in Gujarat. She also promoted the Maheshwar weaving industry, reviving traditional handloom crafts that still thrive today.
s: Thirty years of wise government with care for the common people
Building and restoring temples, ghats, wells and roads across India
Promoting the Maheshwar weaving industry and traditional handloom crafts

questions.q: The chapter says Maratha rule planted the early seeds of India's freedom movement. Apply the chapter's reasoning to explain how a power that ended in 1818 could do that.
questions.a: Sample: What the Marathas left behind was not territory but an example. They had challenged Mughal dominance and built the largest Indian empire before the British, governing it with an efficient administration of their own. Their fight had been driven by the ideal of Swarajya, self-rule, not merely by a wish to change rulers. So even after 1818 Indians could point to a time within memory when Indians had governed India competently, and that belief that they could govern themselves is what the chapter calls the early seed of the freedom movement.
s: Notes what the Marathas achieved: the largest Indian empire before the British, well administered
Identifies Swarajya as the ideal that drove them
Explains how that example later convinced Indians they could govern themselves

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Marathi inscription on a wall of the Brihadishwara temple at Thanjavur is valuable to historians. Reason (R): It records the history of the Bhonsle family and is one of the largest single inscriptions in India. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Analyse why the chapter treats the choice of a language or a script -- Sanskrit on a seal, Marathi in a treatise, Modi in letters -- as a political act and not only a cultural one.
questions.a: Sample: A seal is the mark of authority, so putting a Sanskrit inscription on it where Persian was expected announced that this authority came from a different tradition than the sultanates' or the Mughals'. The Rajya-Vyavahara-Kosha went further and supplied Sanskrit words for the Persian ones used in diplomacy, and the chapter records that foreign loanwords in Maratha diplomacy then fell considerably, so the very vocabulary in which the state spoke to other states changed. The Modi script carried the same independence into everyday correspondence. Each choice decided whose terms the state would conduct its business on, which is a political question.
s: Explains the seal as an announcement of authority on its own terms
Uses the Rajya-Vyavahara-Kosha and the fall in foreign loanwords in diplomacy
Concludes that the language of state business is itself a political choice

questions.q: Tarabai and Ahilyabai Holkar each took charge after the death of her husband. Analyse how differently the two used the power they held, and what each is remembered for.
questions.a: Sample: Tarabai took charge at a moment of war, when Aurangzeb was in the Deccan, and used her power as a strategist: she saw that north India lay unprotected, raised large armies and sent them into Mughal territory, outlasting the Mughal Empire and preserving Maratha independence at a critical time. Ahilyabai Holkar took charge of a settled kingdom around Indore and ruled it for thirty years, using her power to build -- hundreds of temples, ghats, wells and roads from Kedarnath to Rameswaram, and the Maheshwar weaving industry. One is remembered as the architect of the northward expansion, the other as a wise administrator who cared for the common people.
s: Describes Tarabai's military and strategic use of power
Describes Ahilyabai Holkar's administrative and building work
States clearly what each is remembered for

questions.q: Of the contributions listed under 'The Maratha legacy', judge which mattered most to later Indian history, and support your choice from the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter lists four: the largest Indian empire before the British, an efficient new way of governing, the revival of local traditions without religious discrimination, and the ideal of Swarajya. The empire was lost in 1818 and the administration went with it, so neither survived the Marathas. The ideal of Swarajya did survive, because the chapter says it later inspired many Indians to believe they could govern themselves and planted the early seeds for India's freedom movement. Judged by what outlasted Maratha power itself, Swarajya mattered most.
s: Sets out the contributions the chapter actually lists
Chooses one and gives the chapter's evidence for it
Justifies the choice against the alternatives

questions.q: Write the label card for a museum object from Thanjavur under the Marathas. Name the object, say what it is made of or what it shows, and add two lines on why it matters.
questions.a: Sample: 'Thanjavur painting, 19th century. Painted panel with delicate gold foil work that gives the surface a rich, radiant appearance. This style flourished under the patronage of the Thanjavur Marathas, rulers who were themselves poets and dramatists and great patrons of the arts. It belongs to the syncretic culture of the region, where local Tamil, the Telugu of the former rulers and the Marathi of the new ones met and interacted freely.'
s: Names a real object from the chapter and describes it accurately
Written in the form of a museum label
Two lines of significance drawn from the chapter
